newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa shepherds Zairean parties towards talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa shepherds Zairean parties towards talks.

text.p: South Africa made efforts on Friday to shepherd Zaire's warring parties towards peace talks, but sources close to the discussions said progress was slow.
"Things are happening, but if anybody is going to say anything it should be the Zaireans and I don't think that will be before very early next week," said one African source.
Zaire said on Friday its army would not relent in its air offensive against Tutsi-led rebels holding towns and territory in the country's eastern provinces.

Zaire says forces from Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi invaded its territory in support of the four-month-old rebellion, which was sparked by Zairean threats to expel ethnic Tutsis who trace their roots in the country back to the 18th century.

"The Zaire armed forces who received orders to fight and recover captured territories and pacify the country have up to today received no counter-orders to stop fighting," Defence Minister Likulia Bolongo said in a statement.
Ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko was expected at his French Riviera holiday mansion on Friday, possibly for treatment following surgery last year for prostate cancer.
It was not clear whether he planned to use the opportunity to consult other African leaders as he has done during previous visits to France.
U.S. officials in Cape Town confirmed that South Africa was leading proximity talks in a search for peace in Zaire.

Zairean envoy Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba, Mobutu's nephew and chief security adviser, told Radio France Internationale in a telephone interview from Cape Town that South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki was talking to both sides.
"South Africa is...trying to bring points of view together and pass one side's points of view to the other.

"It's not my presence that can be useful, it's the work that (Deputy) President Thabo Mbeki is undertaking through the many contacts he is having with...let's say the presidents of the region...which can move things forward," he said.

South African officials said they were under orders to say nothing about the talks, but a source did confirm that Mandela had been briefed by Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo on a visit to the region and had talked to Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni.
A spokesman for Mbeki said he had left Cape Town on Friday to attend to government duties elsewhere in the country and would not be back before Sunday evening.
"There is no reason why the process should not continue without the deputy president there. It's a government process, not a personal one. There are others involved," he said.
South African officials declined to comment on a statement in New York by a United Nations spokesman that rebel leader Laurent Kabila was expected in Cape Town by the weekend.

A U.S. official in Cape Town said George Moose, assistant secretary of state for African affairs, and U.S. National Security Council official Susan Rice had extended their stay in the city and would be available to bolster the peace process.

"We welcome the effort of South Africa...to begin talks separately with representatives of both sides in the conflict with the aim of trying to determine whether there is a basis for the peaceful resolution of the conflict in Zaire," the official said.

A diplomatic source monitoring the talks in Cape Town said South Africa was working with the Southern African Development Community, the countries of the Great Lakes region around Zaire, the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity to finda framework for peace talks.
"It's not just a South African initiative. It's much wider than that," he said.
